title: Open restriction preserves local constancy
statement: Let $X$ be a scheme [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions], $F$ a locally constant sheaf of sets on its small etale site [def-weil-pbc-etale-sheaves], and $U$ any open subscheme. The set inverse image of $F$ along the inclusion of $U$ [def-weil-pbc-inverse-image] is locally constant on the small etale site of $U$. Neither finite stalks nor Noetherianity is assumed.

proof.text: Identify constancy of F.over V with constancy of its inverse image along V.hom. Use Scheme.Etale.overSheafEquiv, etaleToOverCompForgetIso, fullyFaithfulSheafToPresheaf.preimageIso and the inverse-image restriction comparison to identify the two sheaves. Sheaf.isConstant_sheafCongr_functor_iff transports constancy across the site equivalence and Sheaf.isConstant_congr across the comparison isomorphism. These general constant-sheaf and equivalence interfaces are already proved in WeilConjectures.Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Sites.ConstantSheafEquivalence.

For an etale morphism g, restriction of a constant sheaf to the site localized at Etale.mk g is constant by the proved general library lemma CategoryTheory.Sheaf.isConstant_over (WeilConjectures.Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Sites.ConstantSheaf). The preceding identification makes its set inverse image constant. Apply this to each projection V times_X U to V. Choose the original trivializing cover and base change it using Cover.pullback₂; stability under base change is the precoverage instance.

Use the composition isomorphisms c supplied by the inverse-image composition theorem. The pullback square condition identifies the two composite scheme morphisms, so composing c, eqToIso of that equality, and the inverse of c gives an isomorphism between the two iterated inverse images. Transport constancy with Sheaf.isConstant_congr and then the first-step identification. Every member of the base-changed cover therefore trivializes the inverse image on U, giving local constancy.

proof_origin.place: Open restriction preserves local constancy; Lean implementation by E1 using site localization and inverse-image composition.
